chief_complaint: pain radiating down lateral leg to big toe with foot drop
hpi_details: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with pain radiating down lateral leg to big toe with foot drop. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she severely pulled a tendon or pinched a nerve in her lower back while lifting heavy furniture last weekend.
concerns: She is worried that her foot will give out while waiting tables at work and cause her to collapse in front of customers.
expectations: She hopes to get a temporary brace to keep her foot from catching on the floor and a doctor's note excusing her from standing shifts this week.

clinical_knowledge.topic: L5 radiculopathy from L4-L5 disc herniation: evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of L5 radiculopathy from L4-L5 disc herniation is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Foot drop is a motor deficit that requires urgent lumbar MRI and prompt spine specialist assessment; treatment is tailored to the severity and progression of the deficit.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out L4/L5 Lumbar Radiculopathy.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Peroneal nerve palsy without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Progressive foot drop.
management_principles: Obtain urgent lumbar MRI and arrange prompt spine specialist assessment for foot drop
Assess for cauda equina symptoms and escalating motor weakness
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of pain radiating down lateral leg to big toe with foot drop. HPI: L4/L5 disc herniation compressing L5 nerve root.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for L4/L5 Lumbar Radiculopathy.
reference_soap.assessment: Findings are highly suspicious for L5 radiculopathy, commonly due to L4-L5 disc herniation.
reference_soap.plan: Obtain urgent lumbar MRI and arrange prompt spine specialist assessment for foot drop. Assess for cauda equina symptoms and escalating motor weakness. Use analgesia as appropriate while definitive evaluation is underway.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of L4/L5 Lumbar Radiculopathy
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for L4/L5 Lumbar Radiculopathy
Recognize foot drop as an indication for urgent imaging and spine specialist assessment

teaching.diagnosis: L5 radiculopathy due to L4-L5 disc herniation
teaching.one_liner: A herniated disc compressing the L5 nerve root causing pain down the lateral leg to the big toe with foot drop.
red_flags: New urinary retention or incontinence, bowel dysfunction, saddle numbness, or rapidly worsening bilateral weakness (possible cauda equina syndrome)

must_ask.say: Does the pain go down the outside of your leg to your big toe?
Have you noticed your foot dragging or catching when you walk?
Any numbness on top of your foot?
Any new trouble passing urine, loss of bowel control, or numbness around the groin or buttocks?
How is this affecting your walking?

history.answer: My right leg has a sharp shooting pain running down the outside all the way to my big toe, and my right foot feels weak and keeps dragging.
The pain starts in my right lower back and shoots down the outer side of my right calf onto the top of my foot and big toe.
It started about four days ago right after I lifted several heavy storage boxes, and it has become steadily worse since then.
It feels like a sharp, burning electric shock shooting down my leg, and at its worst it reaches about a seven out of ten.
Sitting down, bending forward, or coughing makes the shooting pain much worse, whereas lying flat with my knees bent gives me slight relief.
If I lie still in bed the pain calms down, and it does not wake me up at night unless I turn over.
No, I do not have any stiffness in the morning, and moving around actually aggravates the pain rather than helping it.
Yes, the outer part of my lower right leg and the top of my foot feel numb and tingly, like they are asleep.
My right foot feels noticeably weak, and the front of my foot drops down and catches on the carpet when I take steps.
No, the feeling between my legs and around my bottom is completely normal.
No, I have had no accidents, no difficulty passing urine, and no problems controlling my bladder or bowels.
Walking is awkward because of my dragging foot, but sitting down or leaning forward makes the sharp pain worse, not better.
No fever, chills, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss, though I do feel worn out from dealing with this pain.
No, I have never had cancer or any tumors.
No, I haven't had any recent infections, spinal injections, procedures, diabetes, or intravenous drug use.
No, I have never taken steroids, I do not have weak bones, and I have not had any major falls or injuries.
No belly pain, no pulsating sensation in my abdomen, and no burning or blood when I urinate.
No eye redness or pain, no heel pain, no chronic diarrhea, and no scaly skin rashes.
I took four hundred milligrams of ibuprofen yesterday, but it barely took the edge off the pain.
I work as a retail stock clerk lifting heavy boxes and standing for long shifts, which has been impossible with this leg pain.
I can barely walk without tripping over my right toes, so I haven't been able to go to work or do simple chores.
I thought I just pulled a tendon or pinched something in my lower back when I was helping my roommate move heavy furniture last weekend.
I'm terrified my foot is going to drag and give out while I'm carrying trays at work and I'll drop everything and fall.
I was hoping you could give me some kind of brace so I stop tripping over my toes, and maybe a note for work so I can sit down.
I have always been healthy and do not have any chronic medical problems.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any daily prescription medications, over-the-counter pills, or dietary supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any nicotine products.
I only have a casual drink on social occasions, maybe one glass of beer once or twice a month.
I live in an apartment with a roommate who has been helping me with meals and groceries since this started.
No one in my family has a history of disc problems, nerve conditions, or autoimmune disease.
My last period started two weeks ago, and my cycles are regular every twenty-eight days.
My partner and I always use condoms, and there is no chance that I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.7°C, oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air.
Alert, comfortable while standing still but winces and avoids bearing weight on the right heel; shifts uncomfortably when seated.

Normal lumbar lordosis without spinal deformity; mild tenderness over right L4-L5 paraspinal musculature; straight-leg raise is positive on the right at 40 degrees reproducing radiating pain down the lateral leg, negative on the left.
Right ankle dorsiflexion and right great toe extension (extensor hallucis longus) are 3/5; right plantarflexion and knee extension are 5/5; left lower extremity motor strength is 5/5 throughout.
Decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick over the right anterolateral lower leg and the dorsum of the right foot including the first web space; sensation is intact on the left leg.
Patellar reflexes (L4) and Achilles reflexes (S1) are 2+ bilaterally and symmetric; plantar reflexes are flexor bilaterally (negative Babinski).
Demonstrates a right-sided steppage gait with inability to walk on the right heel; walking on the toes is preserved.
Normal resting and active anal sphincter tone; intact perianal sensation in the S3 to S5 distribution.
Soft, non-tender, without palpable masses, guarding, or pulsatile midline abdominal expansion.
